title: Poems of Emptiness
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett's main teaching emphasizes the importance of humility and recognizing one's own limitations in the spiritual journey, cautioning against idealizing teachers or students. They draw inspiration from traditional Chinese koans, which suggest that there are no inherent teachers of Zen, only individuals who guide others on their path. By embracing this perspective, we can approach our practice with a sense of curiosity, openness, and peer-to-peer dialogue, recognizing that everyone is both teacher and student in the dharma.

sentences.text: What a sweet, intimate sesshin, huh?
Just us guys hanging out, trying to awaken, whatever that is.
I do really appreciate having sesshin here.
I feel like that's when we're somehow fully, I don't know, actualizing the temple, all the efforts that were involved to create a space where we can do this.
So that just feels really, really good.
I mean, wherever we're here, it's great, but somehow sesshin here is extra special.
So, express our gratitude to our donors, our labor and our love that built this place, turned this accountant office into a practice place.
Well, I think I can probably speak safely for everyone (not often you can speak safely for everyone), but I think I can safely say that we're so touched by your talk.
Wow.
It's a good thing I myself have studied the eight worldly winds, because it appears that you're famous and I'm not.
Full house, which is wonderful, as it should be.

I was interested how much of Juriki's story revolved around teachers: different teachers that he's had in his life, and what he learned from them, and the situations that evolved around them, situations wondrous, traumatic and everywhere in between, with different teachers.
So I thought I might start the talk by trying to say something about the student-teacher relationship, the way I look at it.
This has also come up a lot in dokusan and in other conversations.
And I don't know if this will shed light or just confusion, because I think I have a fairly ambiguous attitude about teachers and students.
And one of the origin points of this is: one time, 20-something years ago, I was in dokusan with Norman.
I think it was the State Street zendo.
And he had just come back from a teacher meeting or something, maybe the American Zen Teachers Association, which he was involved with at the beginning, and I'm in that now.
And he was basically kind of sharing in a collegial kind of way, which really touched me, because I certainly didn't think of myself as a teacher.

And saying how he'd been a little surprised and a little reactive to something his peers had been saying at this teacher meeting: that they'd been talking a lot about "my students this" and "my students that."
And Norman was telling me, if I remember correctly, that something about that possessive pronoun really bothered him.
It didn't feel right to say "my students," as if you possess somebody and kind of control their destiny, or think you have some special something about them.
And then he said, as he said in many settings, "I just feel fortunate to practice with people.
I just don't really think about it that way.

I get to practice with different people in different kinds of ways, and I have different relationships, dharma relations, with different people, but I never feel superior, like I'm the teacher with my students."
And a little bit later than that, maybe 10 years later, he wrote an essay that was influential for me as well, which we have [unclear: "on and onto"] somewhere, called "There Are No Teachers of Zen."
And it was based on a koan, a traditional case from the Shoyoroku, called "Huangbo's Dreg Slurpers."
So here's one translation of this traditional story.
Huangbo is one of the great teachers of the Tang dynasty.
These stories usually star one or the other of...
*Huangbo said to the assembly, "You people are all slurpers of dregs.
If you continue like this, where will you end up?
Do you know that in all of China there are no teachers of Chan, no teachers of Zen?"*
You people are all slurpers of dregs: graspy feeling to it, right?
You carry on like this, or travel like this, that's how you translate that character.
Where will you end up?
What will you have?
Don't you know that in all of China there are no teachers of Zen?
*At that point a monk came forward and said, "What about all those who guide followers and lead groups in various places?"*
Fair question.
*And Huangbo said, "I don't say there's no Zen, just that there are no teachers."*
In his essay exploring this: we need people in all the different roles, but maybe it's not so healthy to privilege one role so strongly as the thing.
And probably this is also a reaction, from Norman and other teachers of his generation growing up in the enthusiastic early era.

He's sort of like maybe the second wave of the early era in the West, where people were so excited about Zen masters and enlightenment, a very sort of intensified and idealized vision, and also a very countercultural vision: that we were going to create a whole new society (which maybe we are anyway) based on something ineffable, unimaginably brilliant and insightful and perfect, a true understanding of all, through enlightenment, as mediated by infallible Zen masters.
Maybe Norman [unclear: "they're making a play"] for, like, let's turn that down.
And that's naturally and organically turning itself down, I think, over the generations.
Maybe I'm the third or fourth generation, or however you count it.
So that's kind of where I started from.
But I want to do a good job. [unclear: "Khan"] wants to do a good job.
We seem to end up with titles and positions in our sangha, and you want to do a good job in your position, in your title, with your title, and with the situation.
Because it's not that there is no Zen.
It's not that there aren't people leading groups and guiding students.
But there are no teachers in that way.
So we don't need ownership and exclusivity, because it's a little hazardous.
What we do need, and have, and hope can continue to grow, is love, a love that's bright and wise and bigger than any of us.

Maybe the problem with the Zen master model is there's some sense there, maybe in the person inhabiting it if they're not careful, and in the projections people place upon that person, that somehow the magic stuff's inside them.
They are the Zen master, they have the understanding.
And we may forget that it's all completely relational and situational and emergent.
The teachers and students manifest teachers and students, and enlighten and enliven the way.
And it's great to have many teachers, right?
We all know this.
Maybe this emerging version of Zen is a little bit polyamorous, or poly-teacherish or something, poly-studentish.
You don't have to be monogamous with your teacher.
I thought of that earlier today.
You'd like it.
That said, it's wonderful to have a strong relationship in the dharma with someone who has gone a little bit before you.
I remember Norman also had a crisis of confidence he shared with us one time, when he received transmission in about 1990.
And he kind of felt like, like you probably would too: I'm just me.
What the heck?
They gave me the special robes and the special titles, and I'm supposed to do the special thing, and I'm just me.
I know I've changed and grown in some ways, but I'm inherently the same old conditioned being I always was, as far as I can tell.

And one of the things that was kind of cool about being around San Francisco Zen Center from the mid 70s to the 2000s, when he was there, is pretty much all the greats in Western Buddhism passed through at one time or another.
In the couple years I was in and out, I met a lot of them too.
So he met a lot, a lot of them.

And one time Thich Nhat Hanh came through, and he didn't get to have an individual conversation with him, but he got to be at a table with 15 people or something, and they all got to ask questions of Thich Nhat Hanh.
I told you this story before, probably.
So he asked about this.
He said, "Thay, I have this rank and title.
I don't really know if I'm legit."
I don't know how he said it exactly.
And Thich Nhat Hanh just spoke to trusting your experience and trusting the dharma.
He said something like, "Oh, it's okay.
Ten-year person can help five-year person.
Three-month person help one person." [unclear: "And he gives english local about that way"], that was reported to me, without so many articles, anything.
So you just help as you can.
And if you've been around, you help this person who came in the door behind you.
You turn around, right?
Oh, welcome, please come here.
And you practice humility over and over and over again, because you only know so much, and you don't know what you don't know, right?
That's the thing about knowing: you literally can't know what you don't know.
So my sense has always been that we should hold teachers and students lightly, and treasure it nonetheless.
It is the treasure of our tradition that we help each other, and then we turn around at the door and welcome the next person in, however that looks.

And then we have a little bit of confusion, which probably will never be clarified, a little bit of ambiguity in our particular school, our lineage, around what about priests and lay people, so-called.
This is a problem we inherited from Japan, which has a married clergy.

All the schools of Buddhism pretty much, there are a few little fringy ones that have true monastics, who do take the lifetime vow of celibacy and poverty and obedience, like all the other hardcore monastics.
But for the most part, clergy in Japan are a married clergy.
So what's the difference, really, between an ordained person around here and a lay person?
I've got a house, and married.
And to make it even more confusing, my wife is also married and ordained, luckily to me, so I guess that helps.
So what's really the difference?
I bring this up partly because I'm noticing that I do feel a difference, but I don't know how to describe it in a way that's ever fair or correct or complete.
In the process of ordaining, we have some higher expectations, or other expectations: an ethic, practice, and maybe more study.
Simply sewing the darn robe is a thing.
And Norman never expressed very clearly his expectations of his ordained students.
We got the famed (because I repeat it constantly) three points, which are so good, but they're good for everybody, right?
The three points: be humble, see everyone as Buddha, and try to help.
That's really good.
Everyone should practice that way.
But Norman's expectations would sometimes kind of leak around the edges.

Like, one time I was on the phone with him about an upcoming sesshin, and he said to me, "Where's so-and-so?" referring to one of my peers, another enlightened, I'm not enlightened, sorry, where'd that come from?
Another ordained, ordained here.
Oh, we're all enlightened, so I guess that's okay.
Anyway.
So, "How about so-and-so?
Is she coming?"
And I said, "No, no, she's not coming."
And Norman said, "Gosh darn it, she didn't come last time either.
I really expect you guys to come to all the retreats."
Like, oh, you never told us that.
And the first couple of people I ordained, I followed his lead.
I didn't express any expectations.
And it got a little complicated with a few of them, because I realized I had expectations, and that was pretty much unfair, to have them and expect something and not tell anybody.
We've all been in relationships like that, right?
It doesn't go well.
So I created a list of expectations for ordained people.
It seems reasonable to me.
Well, I've never wanted to create, or felt an interest in creating, such a list for not-ordained people, even for people who are serious practitioners here.
I do say, maybe Chris is about the same, I don't know, she'd probably have a different version of all this, which is fine.
I do say, if you do jukai and receive the precepts, you're committing to something.
This is not just a fun little thing to do.
You're committing to precepts, for sure.
You're warming up your relationship to the sangha.
You know that you're doing this not just for you, but also for the sangha.
And I usually say it warms up your relationship with the preceptor, with the teacher you're receiving this from.
But it doesn't need to be exclusive, or any kind of permanent.
And you probably wouldn't want to receive precepts from somebody you thought was a creep.
Someone you respect, who's representing the lineage.
So I feel like in jukai I'm representing the lineage as best I can, and welcoming people into the family.
It feels maybe more like being an uncle than the dad, or something.
But for whatever reason, with priest ordination, yeah, it's more like being the dad, not literally.
And I wrote down expectations.
And such a person, I would certainly expect, would listen to their ordination teacher closely, especially for the first five years, where you're really sort of actively training and learning.
And we don't exactly have a five-year curriculum or a seminary or anything.

But I put on my little thing that it's a lifetime relationship, which I think is really true: that even 10 or 15 or 20 years later, maybe you would reach out to your ordination teacher if something [unclear: "some miss"] in your life, or you wanted to do some different thing, especially a thing in the dharma.
Hey, I was thinking about purple rakusus, everything about that, whatever.
Some people do that.
So this does seem like a teacher-student relationship that's pretty inherently strong and close.
But recently we have had, Chris and I both have had people come to us, and they're not ordained, and they're like, "I really want to, okay if I go talk to the other one?
Would that be betraying you?
Would your feelings get hurt?"
And we're really happy when they ask, because, please go ahead!
Goodness gracious. [unclear: "See if all of us"], why did you get that idea?
But it's in the air, right?
It's in the water: I found my teacher, and I should be loyal to him or her, only talk about intimate dharma concerns with that person.
Interestingly, there is actually no traditional Soto ceremony (and the ceremonies are really when things are formalized), there's no Soto Zen ceremony for "can I become your teacher?"
Quite a few Western lineages, and most of the ones I visited in Oregon earlier this year, do use one.
It seems to be adapted from a Rinzai ceremony that's done when a monk is entering the monastery for training and sort of formally asks the abbot for admission.
But then in a lot of cases, in the big training monasteries, they don't ever get to talk to the abbot again after that.
So it's not the same thing.
So we do this much more informally, for the most part, in a relaxed, cheerful spirit.
And I usually say organically: a teacher-student relationship, like any relationship, right, grows and changes organically.
Organic growth.

But actually, maybe the whole sort of confusing thing about priests and lay people being different, but not being different, is spot on, because maybe it kind of mirrors our deep teachings on form and emptiness.
There are priests.
They're identifiable, because there's special clothes and haircuts and stuff, and because we just know that they are.
Word gets out.
And there are committed lay people.
They have different markings and designations.
And the priests are making some kind of big commitment to carry forward a certain kind of archetype of monastic practice, even though they aren't completely monastics.
So there's a thing there.
There's a form, right?
The priests are holding a form, form practice.
There's something to it, and something to it that we've received, generation after generation.
That stuff's kind of true.
But it's also completely empty, and doesn't have any inherent actual anything to it, right?
We're all just people.
We're playing.
It's an elaborate cosplay, religious cosplay, that we're taking seriously and holding lightly.
And there's no difference between priests and lay people, between me and you, or each other.
So anyway, maybe it's a great thing to stay confused about.
I just don't know if this helped the conversation or not.
But I think the main thing is just to have conversations, not to assume, and to talk to each other.
Come to dokusan a lot.
Talk to each other as peers.
Ask questions, be curious, and don't assume anything.
There's stuff in us from that enthusiastic early literature of Zen.
We can't help it.
Maybe a little less so now, but when I was starting, pretty much every single person I knew who was starting Zen had read a whole bunch of books, and that's how they knew about it.
And so they were kind of looking for what they read about in the books, and sometimes that was a little confusing, because they wouldn't see it exactly that way.
But the other thing about all this is, everyone is your teacher, right?
And all of us are students.
That's a deep reality of all of this.
And all that said, if you want to think of me or Kanho as your teacher, that's great.
We're happy.
That's helpful.
Not helpful?
Please forget about it.

And also, the way we're doing things in our lineage (and this is a Western creation, a couple decades old), just to make it even more interesting, we then empower experienced and committed lay practitioners as lay entrusted teachers.
So if you have a good relationship with Hannah or Talus or John or Reizan Bob, you could say, would you be my teacher?
They'll say something humble first, I hope, and then they'll say, yeah, sure.
So how lucky we are to have six people holding this formless rank of teacher.
It's a big T.
The number will probably just increase if we keep going the way we're going.
How lucky. [unclear: "Some support about the ways to get confused."] We just want to get confused in the ways that we grow and learn.
But also, luckily, we don't have any Zen masters.
We can leave that in the rear view, and we can enjoy it in the beautiful literature of them.
We can treasure the Zen master as a wonderful idea, a trope, an archetype and a vision, but maybe we don't have conditioned people trying to play that role.
We can keep that in a safer place.

But most importantly, the most important of all of this (forget about everything I just said, here's the important part): we most definitely, measurably and demonstrably true, have here a solid and growing group of thoughtful, deeply committed practitioners of the way.
A good part of the core of that group are right here, right now.
I really admire that.
I admire all of you.
I'm really grateful and touched.
And I hope, when I'm in the teacher's seat, which is glued to my butt or something, I'll cause more help than confusion.
I hope so.
And I appreciate feedback.
I'm trying to learn the wisdom of when the feedback is something I should take on and look at, and when it's actually your stuff.
But give it to me anyway.
Don't try to figure that out.
Tell me, and we'll look at it together.
In the best world, we'll look at it together.
Best, best world, we'll look at it together, say, look at that reaction, let's look at it.
So this form and emptiness thing, though, isn't just an aside in our tradition.
It's so central.
It's central to us every moment of every day.
And it's hard for our thinking minds to open to the teachings of form and emptiness.
So I thought we'd explore that a little bit today, and then I'll hopefully stop before I go on too long.
Another great blessing of Juriki's talk is, now I hopefully will no longer get complaints, complaints about my long talks.
I need to say, yeah, well, you enjoyed Juriki's, right?
So I've got nothing on him.
And actually a couple people did tell me, I usually don't like long talks; I was really captured.
Somebody sent me a beautiful poem.

This is actually from the Korean Zen tradition, the school of Seung Sahn, started by the Korean monk (I also actually got to meet him one time in San Francisco Zen Center, very powerful, fierce kind of dude).
Anyway, this is from the 14th century.
It's a Korean monk named Naong.
Naong.
The title is "The Human Route," or "The Human Path."
*Coming empty-handed,* sorry, *coming empty-handed, going empty-handed, that is a human.
When you were born, where did you come from?
When you die, where do you go?
Like a floating cloud which appears,* I'm sorry, *life is like a floating cloud which appears.
Death is like a floating cloud which disappears.
The floating cloud itself originally does not exist.
Life and death, coming and going, are also like that.
But there is one thing which always remains clear.
It is pure and clear, not depending on life and death.
Tell me, what is the one pure and clear thing?*
It's not giving anything away, this guy.
Feel into this, though.
It's a powerful sort of way to explore emptiness, through the poetry of emptiness of the great Zen masters.
*Coming empty-handed, going empty-handed, that is human.
When you are born, where do you come from?
When you die, where do you go?
Life is like a floating cloud which appears.
Death is like a floating cloud which disappears.
The floating cloud itself originally does not exist.
Life and death, coming and going, are all like that.
There is one thing which always remains clear.
It is pure and clear, not depending on life and death.
What is the one pure and clear thing?*
So that's our practice: to inquire into the mystery.
One time I had a period where I just kind of felt, I kind of had low-level grouchy kind of suffering.
Everything was sort of fine in my life, as far as I knew, and I went to see Norman, and he said, "Oh, you should study emptiness."
I guess I was shy or something.
I didn't ask him how to do it.
I'm like, oh, okay, thank you.
I've been wondering about that ever since.
How do you study emptiness?
I wonder, if I'd ask him, if he'd remember that exchange.
Probably not.
"Did I say that?"
So the world of form, the relative world, is what we can talk about and think about, right?
The world of concepts and relationships, and this is bigger than that, and that's smaller than this, and I'm not me and you're not you, and blah blah blah blah.
The world of words, the world of all these teachings, the world of the relative.
And yet that's not the whole world.
We can feel this.
We can intuit this, or we would never have come here.

It's also a world of incompleteness, a world of suffering, a world of disconnection and a world of pain, that needs the light from behind, from beyond concepts, beyond thinking, beyond narrowing things down to this word or that word, beyond comparison, better or worse, or this or that.
There's the world of freedom.
And it's not like we're trying to get out of one world and into the other world, because that would be really nice, and just sort of check out there.
Sometimes the early teachings might be read that way: arhats are trying to pop off into nirvana or something.
But that's not really quite what they meant by it.
This really matters for our studies, the study of form and emptiness: to feel into what's beyond my view, what's beyond my conceptualization.
The practice of sesshin is for sure a great help in all this.
And I think practice from sesshin can help in two or three different ways, depending how you think about it, help us to recognize this interpenetration of the two worlds.
This is the teaching of the two worlds.
And there's lots of different terms that are used, and you might not like the word emptiness.
It's just what I grew up on, so I use it.
Maybe you like boundlessness, or spaciousness, or something like that, or interbeing, Thich Nhat Hanh also said, the ultimate.
I kind of like form and emptiness, relative and absolute.
It's just easy for me to say those words.
Because it doesn't matter, actually, right?
Because we're trying to point to something beyond words, so we don't need to worry about which words they are.
But you can use words that you find the most helpful in your journey to appreciating the beyond-words of all this life and all of this love.
Anyway, one thing sesshin does that I think helps is it actually intensifies the relative world.
People say this, right?
They say sesshin is intense.
They don't often say sesshin is blissful and peaceful, for some reason.
You may have had experiences like that in sesshin, but if you ask them, how was sesshin?
Oh, wow.
Pretty intense.
And I think it's something of the function of practice, the structure, the container, doing a lot more zazen, the shared intention, where actually it's not like we leave the relative world behind.
It just gets stronger and more intense.
Our interactions with our thoughts, and with each other, become actually more powerful, because we're more focused, and we're more present, and we're more quiet, right?

So the few words that are expressed, whether verbally or on little notes, or all that non-verbal shenanigans that's happening all the time, right, communicate many things and miscommunicate many things.
It gets more intense, which gives us such powerful opportunities to practice, because we see more clearly.
Wow.
Sometimes the wow has a lot of confusion and pain in it for us, when we're surprised by something or shocked by something or upset by something.
Because in the silence, a few words ring loud, and we become more vulnerable, and more open, and softer too.
So the intenseness: we don't have our armor on.
Sometimes our armor sort of softens and sloughs off when we're not looking, and then somebody pokes us, deliberately or not, and, yeah, those usually bounce off, and that went right to the gut.
Ouch.
So from there, the question is, can we practice with this?
What can we learn?
How can we grow?
And this doesn't mean that we lose the realm of appropriate and inappropriate, and that we aren't trying to sort of arrange things in the best way possible.
It's a little unfortunate, and too easy, to be a little glib if you're not the one reacting.
Someone brings their reaction, and you might be tempted (I admit to having done this recently), you might be tempted to say something like, oh, you can practice with that, right?
So that's still a real thing.
Some things are inappropriate, and they hurt, and we shouldn't do them.
It's a shame.
This is not open season.
I just thought if I startled you, you'd wake up.
And plenty of Zen master stories like that too, right?
Hitting and shouting and shocking people.
Maybe they'll wake up, because the Zen master can read your mind and knows which synapses need to fire.
So it's not like that.
Of course we're careful.
We're as kind and gentle as we can be with each other.
But we're still going to have stuff to learn in the relative world in sesshin.
And the first thing we can notice is where we go with it.
There's a lot of places we could go with it.
We could try to fix it.
We could reach out to the leadership and try to get that person straightened out, or something.
Sometimes that's right, sometimes not, hard to say.
Sometimes we swallow it, in a way that's healthy, or swallow it in a way that's unhealthy.
Sometimes we fight back.
Less so now, but there were times in the happily distant past where nasty notes would go back and forth.
May that not be true again, practicing silence.
And sometimes, when conditions are right, we can practice with emptiness.
The conditions have to be right.
Somehow we have to be karmically ready in the relative world, and you can't make it happen.
But you can be curious whether it's possible.
You can be ready.
You can be ready to be surprised by your own non-reaction, your own letting go, your own wisdom self arising.
The possibility, keeping with this note example, because there's notes, to be able to see, oh, just words, squiggles on the paper.
I don't need to take that on.
And usually it's a mix of the two, right?
Oh, that hurts.
Okay, how do I practice with this?
And sometimes you have to really let it take you to the bottom.
I think that's inevitably true, and maybe an essential part of the learning about form and emptiness in the sesshin: sometimes form just has got to grind you under its good will.
Just how it seems to go.
So here's an example from my life.
One time at Samish sesshin, where I was kind of doing my usual thing, running around, Mr.

Leader, doing it all (my conditioning, I can't help it, I've tried to learn to do it last), and it was, I think, during the meal or right after the meal, and we were in the dining hall at Samish sesshin, and something troubled me.
And usually in my self-talk, my intentions are explicit and good.
So something was a little chaotic or a little unsettled, and I thought to myself, boy, maybe I could just say a few words, make an announcement, and it would help people feel something deeper here.
I don't remember what it was, but I'll just say for the example that it was noise with the spoons and bowls.
That's a common one, guys.
It's so loud in there sometimes you can hardly hear yourself think, to me.
That's what it was, maybe.
I said, I'm sure I was trying to have a very calm voice, "Excuse me, please remember to be quiet with your silverware."
And maybe some people appreciated that.
It's possible.
That's the funny thing about making an announcement: you have no idea how that went in.
You might find out something later.
But my intention was, let's go deeper, let's be more settled, let's be more present, let's feel the deep stillness in the middle of all things.
Let's appreciate emptiness.
But maybe I was a little stuck in the relative when I was trying to make that move.
Anyway, that was a little reactive too: loud in here, if that was what it was.
And there were a fair number of notes back then.

And so a little bit later I went to check my notes, and there was one that said, and I'm pretty sure I remember these words verbatim how many years later, 15 years later: "Maybe sometimes less is more.
Please, can we have fewer announcements?"
And it was unsigned.
And it hit me just to the core.
I felt deeply, deeply criticized.
I felt like a fraud.
Oh boy, just bringing this back up, I can feel it.
My inner unworthiness came racing forward like a freight train, and I just kind of broke down.

And actually, I don't do this often, maybe just a few times in my life, I found a friend, kind of walking in a daze on the lawn, so upset, and I kind of grabbed a friend and took her with me into [unclear: "the focus on her own"], where I just sobbed and unloaded.
Cried and cried and cried, talked and talked and talked.
And I think, of course, it wasn't just about the note.
It was years of tension and years of trying too hard, all erupting, this huge release of energy.
Through the process of that, I could kind of watch a little journey happening to me, more or less, but mostly by thinking about it later.
At the time, I was so caught in the middle of all this.
I definitely started out very caught, very caught, very much in the relative world, big time.
That was hurtful.
Words are powerful.
That was triggering.
Defensive words came to me: don't you know how hard I work for this sangha, how hard I'm trying to make this better?
Some ways of blame, and pushing back at my unknown critic, wondering who it was.
Wouldn't you wonder?
But then, as I sunk into it, sunk into it, I dropped out of narrative, and it was more like just being with pain.
And I could try to categorize the pain, but I don't know if it needs categorizing.
